A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CVPT study, with readable text, equations, figures and tables. All end matter was inspected, including v1's appended NeurIPS checklist. Neither supplied file contains a separate technical appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification and segmentation results, computational-efficiency measurements, prompt-count experiments and cross-attention ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds dataset-specific prompt-count results and expanded initialization/freezing controls.

M1.justification: Both versions use image tokens as queries and prompts as keys/values, insert residual cross-attention between self-attention and the MLP, initialize its frozen weights from self-attention, and train prompts plus the classifier. The revised explanation and additional ablation variants do not change the proposed CVPT procedure.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same 19 VTAB-1K datasets, five FGVC datasets and ADE20K segmentation task. v2's additional CIFAR, DTD and SUN397 analysis uses datasets already covered; it introduces no distinct population, task or input scenario.

E2.justification: The VTAB and FGVC comparisons add RLRR, DM-LoRA, VAPT, VFPT and SA2VP. FGVC additionally adds LoRA and removes Bias; VTAB removes NOAH. SPT-Adapter disappears from all three benchmark comparisons, while ADE20K adds VPT+Bias. These substantially revise the evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: The main VTAB prompt search expands from [1, 5, 10, 20] to [1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200], materially changing model selection and parameter budgets. The expanded weight-sharing experiment also introduces a controlled initialization-by-trainability design. Dataset coverage, backbone families and evaluation metrics remain stable; the reported changes do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds dataset-specific prompt-count sensitivity results in Table 5. Table 6 expands v1's learnable-without-sharing versus frozen-with-sharing comparison into random/pretrained initialization crossed with learnable/frozen attention, plus linear probing. This separates factors previously changed together. The aggregate prompt sweep and placement ablation are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Removing v1's checklist acknowledgment of absent statistical-significance reporting does not change the reporting practice.

E6.justification: Reported CVPT VTAB accuracy changes from 76.2 to 77.2 with parameters increasing from 0.10M to 0.39M under the expanded search; FGVC accuracy changes from 90.3 to 90.5. New comparator and diagnostic results substantially expand the evidence, and the weight-sharing outcomes are revised. CVPT's ADE20K scores and aggregate prompt-sweep table remain unchanged. v2's claimed 12 overall and five structured prompt-method wins exceed Table 1's 11 and four, respectively, counting ties.

T1.justification: The cross-attention definition, CVPT forward equations and quadratic-versus-linear scaling argument remain equivalent. The new attention discussion is conceptual, without new formal assumptions, theorems or proofs. Removing the generic adapter formula shortens background exposition rather than changing the mathematical contribution.

C1.justification: The central contribution—making prompt tuning competitive through cross-attention and weight sharing—is retained. v2 drops lack of visual adaptation as a separate claimed root cause and narrows the introduction's FGVC-and-ADE20K state-of-the-art assertion to OOD tasks such as ADE20K; its FGVC discussion now acknowledges trailing DM-LoRA.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the language-versus-vision semantic-mismatch rationale with a fuller account of prompt deployment and attention allocation, relating it to attention sinks and register tokens. It adds interpretations about preserving general features, contextual features near self-attention, and initialization as an inductive bias. The initialization limitation changes from unexplored potential improvements to reported attempts without substantial benefits.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly specifies ten prompts for the weight-sharing ablation and changes the advertised code repository address from Xlgsyzp/CVPT to Lingyun0419/CVPT. It removes the CIFAR-100 identification from the otherwise retained efficiency-plot caption. Hardware and optimizer disclosures remain essentially unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around attention sinks, ViT registers and previous approaches to excessive attention, contrasting attention redistribution with decoupling prompts. It also incorporates APT, newer PEFT competitors, and work on prompt initialization and transfer behavior. The generic adapter discussion and NOAH citation are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, motivation and conclusion are extensively rewritten. VPT analysis becomes a standalone section, method components receive separate subsections, and the VPT comparison moves into the experiments section. The title is simplified, acknowledgments are added and the appended checklist is removed.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, substantially resizing and relocating figures and tables. Figure 1 is redrawn and moved to the opening page; a dataset-specific sensitivity table is added, and the weight-sharing table is expanded and reorganized. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 modestly strengthens the paper: Table 6 separates initialization from trainability, addressing a confound in v1's central weight-sharing experiment, while updated comparators qualify the earlier FGVC superiority claim. The organization and research context also improve. These benefits are limited by unchanged sparse statistical reporting and the new discrepancy between claimed VTAB win counts and Table 1. The higher VTAB score uses a larger prompt search and does not demonstrate an improved algorithm.
